## Keep Sine and Cosine Together

Consider the integral

$$
\int e^{2x}\sin x\,dx.
$$

Integration by parts can handle it. But differentiating sine produces cosine, and differentiating cosine brings sine back. This suggests keeping the two functions together from the start.

Euler's formula does exactly that:

$$
e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x,
\qquad i^2=-1.
$$

Multiplying by $e^{2x}$ gives

$$
e^{(2+i)x}=e^{2x}\cos x+i e^{2x}\sin x.
$$

One complex function now holds both real integrands. We can integrate it once, then separate its real and imaginary parts.

The same idea will work with polynomial factors. It also works with products of nonnegative integer powers of sine and cosine. The useful step is to turn those products into a finite sum of exponentials.

## Integrating a Complex Exponential

Throughout this note, $x$ is real. A complex-valued function is just a pair of real-valued functions:

$$
f(x)=u(x)+iv(x).
$$

We differentiate and integrate its two parts separately. Thus, if $F'=f$, then

$$
(\operatorname{Re}F)'=u,
\qquad
(\operatorname{Im}F)'=v.
$$

Here $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Im}$ mean real part and imaginary part. No complex integration path is needed.

For a fixed $\omega\in\mathbb C$,

$$
\frac{d}{dx}e^{\omega x}=\omega e^{\omega x}.
$$

When $\omega\ne0$, it follows that

$$
\int e^{\omega x}\,dx
=\frac{e^{\omega x}}{\omega}+K.
$$

The constant $K$ may be complex. Its real and imaginary parts give separate real constants of integration. Below, $C$ denotes an arbitrary real constant in a real-valued answer.

## One Calculation Gives Two Integrals

Take $\omega=2+i$. Since

$$
\frac1{2+i}=\frac{2-i}{5},
$$

we have

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\frac{e^{(2+i)x}}{2+i}=\frac{e^{2x}}5\bigl[(2\cos x+\sin x)+i(2\sin x-\cos x)\bigr].
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{e^{(2+i)x}}{2+i}
&=\frac{e^{2x}}5
\bigl[(2\cos x+\sin x)\\
&\qquad+i(2\sin x-\cos x)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

Taking the real and imaginary parts gives

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int e^{2x}\cos x\,dx=\frac{e^{2x}}5(2\cos x+\sin x)+C
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int e^{2x}\cos x\,dx\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{2x}}5(2\cos x+\sin x)+C
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

and

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int e^{2x}\sin x\,dx=\frac{e^{2x}}5(2\sin x-\cos x)+C.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int e^{2x}\sin x\,dx\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{2x}}5(2\sin x-\cos x)+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

The denominator $5$ is $|2+i|^2$. It appears when we divide by $2+i$, rather than from a separate integration rule.

More generally, let $a,b\in\mathbb R$ with $a^2+b^2>0$. The same calculation gives

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int e^{ax}\cos(bx)\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}}{a^2+b^2}\bigl[a\cos(bx)+b\sin(bx)\bigr]+C,
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int e^{ax}\cos(bx)\,dx\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{ax}}{a^2+b^2}
\bigl[a\cos(bx)\\
&\qquad\qquad\quad+b\sin(bx)\bigr]+C,
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int e^{ax}\sin(bx)\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}}{a^2+b^2}\bigl[a\sin(bx)-b\cos(bx)\bigr]+C.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int e^{ax}\sin(bx)\,dx\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{ax}}{a^2+b^2}
\bigl[a\sin(bx)\\
&\qquad\qquad\quad-b\cos(bx)\bigr]+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

These formulas also cover $a=0$ or $b=0$, provided they are not both zero. If both are zero, the cosine integrand is $1$ and the sine integrand is $0$. We integrate those directly.

## Adding a Polynomial Factor

Now consider the pair

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int (x+1)e^{2x}\cos x\,dx,\qquad \int (x+1)e^{2x}\sin x\,dx.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{gathered}
\int (x+1)e^{2x}\cos x\,dx,\\
\int (x+1)e^{2x}\sin x\,dx.
\end{gathered}
$$

:::
::::

Again, combine them into one integral:

$$
\int (x+1)e^{\omega x}\,dx,
\qquad \omega=2+i.
$$

Integration by parts still plays a role. It now acts on a polynomial and a single exponential. With $u=x+1$ and $dv=e^{\omega x}\,dx$,

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int (x+1)e^{\omega x}\,dx
&=\frac{(x+1)e^{\omega x}}{\omega}-\frac1\omega\int e^{\omega x}\,dx\\
&=e^{\omega x}\left(\frac{x+1}{\omega}-\frac1{\omega^2}\right)+K.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int (x+1)e^{\omega x}\,dx\\
&\quad=\frac{(x+1)e^{\omega x}}{\omega}\\
&\qquad-\frac1\omega\int e^{\omega x}\,dx\\
&\quad=e^{\omega x}
\left(\frac{x+1}{\omega}-\frac1{\omega^2}\right)+K.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

For $\omega=2+i$,

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\frac{x+1}{\omega}-\frac1{\omega^2}=\frac{(10x+7)-i(5x+1)}{25}.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{x+1}{\omega}-\frac1{\omega^2}\\
&\quad=\frac{(10x+7)-i(5x+1)}{25}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

Multiplying by $e^{2x}(\cos x+i\sin x)$ now gives both answers:

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-long}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int (x+1)e^{2x}\cos x\,dx=\frac{e^{2x}}{25}\bigl[(10x+7)\cos x+(5x+1)\sin x\bigr]+C,
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int (x+1)e^{2x}\cos x\,dx\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{2x}}{25}
\bigl[(10x+7)\cos x\\
&\qquad\qquad+(5x+1)\sin x\bigr]+C,
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-long}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int (x+1)e^{2x}\sin x\,dx=\frac{e^{2x}}{25}\bigl[(10x+7)\sin x-(5x+1)\cos x\bigr]+C.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int (x+1)e^{2x}\sin x\,dx\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{2x}}{25}
\bigl[(10x+7)\sin x\\
&\qquad\qquad-(5x+1)\cos x\bigr]+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

The polynomial factor changes the coefficients of sine and cosine. It does not change the basic form of the answer.

## The General Polynomial Formula

Let $P$ be a polynomial of degree at most $d$, where $d\geq0$, and let $\omega\ne0$. Repeated integration by parts gives

$$
\int P(x)e^{\omega x}\,dx
=e^{\omega x}Q(x)+K,
$$

where

$$
Q(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}
\frac{(-1)^kP^{(k)}(x)}{\omega^{k+1}}.
$$

The notation $P^{(k)}$ means the $k$th derivative, with $P^{(0)}=P$. The sum ends because $P^{(d+1)}=0$.

For example, the first terms are

$$
Q=\frac P\omega-\frac{P'}{\omega^2}
+\frac{P''}{\omega^3}-\cdots.
$$

There is also a direct way to understand the formula. Differentiating the proposed answer gives

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(e^{\omega x}Q(x)\bigr)=e^{\omega x}\bigl(\omega Q(x)+Q'(x)\bigr).
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(e^{\omega x}Q(x)\bigr)\\
&\quad=e^{\omega x}\bigl(\omega Q(x)+Q'(x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

So the whole integration problem reduces to finding a polynomial $Q$ such that

$$
\omega Q+Q'=P.
$$

Our finite sum solves this equation. The derivatives cancel in pairs, leaving only $P$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check the Cancellation"}

Multiplying the sum by $\omega$ gives

$$
\omega Q=\sum_{k=0}^{d}
\frac{(-1)^kP^{(k)}}{\omega^k}.
$$

Since $P^{(d+1)}=0$, differentiating and shifting the index gives

$$
Q'=\sum_{k=1}^{d}
\frac{(-1)^{k-1}P^{(k)}}{\omega^k}.
$$

For each $k\geq1$, the coefficients add to zero. The remaining $k=0$ term is $P$. This proves the formula, including the constant-polynomial case.

:::

If $\omega=0$, the integrand is just $P(x)$. Use ordinary polynomial integration. We must not divide by a zero frequency.

## Turning Trigonometric Products into Exponentials

The next step is to handle more than one trigonometric factor. Euler's formula gives

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\sin t=\frac{e^{it}-e^{-it}}{2i},\quad \cos t=\frac{e^{it}+e^{-it}}2.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin t&=\frac{e^{it}-e^{-it}}{2i},\\
\cos t&=\frac{e^{it}+e^{-it}}2.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

After substituting these expressions, a product of sines and cosines becomes a sum of exponentials. Multiplying exponentials just adds their exponents.

This is the link to the polynomial formula. Each term has the form $P(x)e^{\omega x}$, which we already know how to integrate.

### The Same Identity in Hyperbolic Notation

For complex $z$, define

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\sinh z=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}2,\quad \cosh z=\frac{e^z+e^{-z}}2.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sinh z&=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}2,\\
\cosh z&=\frac{e^z+e^{-z}}2.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

Then

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\sin t=-i\sinh(it),\quad \cos t=\cosh(it).
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin t&=-i\sinh(it),\\
\cos t&=\cosh(it).
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

This is another notation for the same conversion. For a nonnegative integer $m$, the whole sine expression must be raised to the power:

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-short}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\sin^m t=[-i\sinh(it)]^m=(-i)^m[\sinh(it)]^m.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin^m t
&=[-i\sinh(it)]^m\\
&=(-i)^m[\sinh(it)]^m.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

The factor is $(-i)^m$, not a single $-i$ for every power. Writing the exponentials directly often makes this factor easier to track.

## A Product Example

Consider the integral

$$
I=\int (x+1)e^{2x}\sin x\cos(3x)\,dx.
$$

Expanding the two trigonometric factors gives

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin x\cos(3x)
&=\frac1{4i}\bigl[e^{4ix}-e^{-4ix}-e^{2ix}+e^{-2ix}\bigr]\\
&=\frac12\bigl[\sin(4x)-\sin(2x)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sin x\cos(3x)\\
&\quad=\frac1{4i}\bigl[e^{4ix}-e^{-4ix}\\
&\qquad\qquad-e^{2ix}+e^{-2ix}\bigr]\\
&\quad=\frac12\bigl[\sin(4x)-\sin(2x)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

The product has split into two frequencies, $4$ and $2$. The last equality is also a product-to-sum identity. Here it follows directly from multiplying exponentials.

For each real $b$, use the polynomial from the general formula:

$$
Q_b(x)=\frac{x+1}{2+ib}-\frac1{(2+ib)^2}.
$$

Define the particular antiderivative

$$
F_b(x)=\operatorname{Im}\bigl[e^{(2+ib)x}Q_b(x)\bigr].
$$

Then $F_b'(x)=(x+1)e^{2x}\sin(bx)$. Using $b=4$ and $b=2$ gives

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
F_4(x)=\frac{e^{2x}}{100}\bigl[(10x+13)\sin(4x)-(20x+16)\cos(4x)\bigr],
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&F_4(x)\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{2x}}{100}
\bigl[(10x+13)\sin(4x)\\
&\qquad\qquad-(20x+16)\cos(4x)\bigr],
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
F_2(x)=\frac{e^{2x}}8\bigl[2(x+1)\sin(2x)-(2x+1)\cos(2x)\bigr].
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&F_2(x)\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{2x}}8
\bigl[2(x+1)\sin(2x)\\
&\qquad\qquad-(2x+1)\cos(2x)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

Therefore the required answer is

$$
I=\frac{F_4(x)-F_2(x)}2+C.
$$

Keeping the answer in two pieces shows where each frequency comes from. It also makes the result easier to check: differentiate each piece, then use the same product-to-sum identity.

## The Full Method

The general integrand has the form

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
f(x)=P(x)e^{cx}\prod_{m=1}^{M}\sin(a_mx)^{t_m}\prod_{j=1}^{J}\cos(b_jx)^{r_j}.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)=P(x)e^{cx}&\prod_{m=1}^{M}\sin(a_mx)^{t_m}\\
&{}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{J}\cos(b_jx)^{r_j}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

Here $P$ is a real polynomial. The frequencies $a_m,b_j$ and the parameter $c$ are real. The powers $t_m,r_j$ are nonnegative integers.

Those integer powers matter. Expanding them uses only finite products and finite binomial sums. No infinite series is needed. An empty product is understood to be $1$.

Let $S$ be the finite set of real frequencies in the expansion. The trigonometric product can be written as

$$
\sum_{\nu\in S}\alpha_\nu e^{i\nu x}.
$$

Here $\nu$ is a frequency in $S$, and $\alpha_\nu$ is its coefficient. The coefficient may be complex. Hence

$$
f(x)=\sum_{\nu\in S}
\alpha_\nu P(x)e^{(c+i\nu)x}.
$$

We can now follow one procedure:

1. Replace each sine and cosine by its exponential expression.
2. Expand the finite products and collect equal frequencies.
3. Integrate each term using the polynomial formula. If $c+i\nu=0$, integrate that polynomial term directly.
4. Combine the results and use Euler's formula to return to real functions.

Since $f$ is real-valued, we may take the real part of the resulting complex primitive. Its derivative is still $f$. After combining terms, a real answer can be written as

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
e^{cx}\sum_{\nu\in S}\bigl[A_\nu(x)\cos(\nu x)+B_\nu(x)\sin(\nu x)\bigr]+C,
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
e^{cx}\biggl[&\sum_{\nu\in S}
A_\nu(x)\cos(\nu x)\\
&+\sum_{\nu\in S}
B_\nu(x)\sin(\nu x)\biggr]+C,
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

with real polynomials $A_\nu$ and $B_\nu$. A zero frequency contributes a polynomial when $c=0$. That term may have degree one higher than $P$.

For a single sine or cosine factor, there is no need to expand a whole product. We can start with $P(x)e^{(c+ib)x}$ and take its imaginary or real part, just as in the first two examples.

## Definite Integrals Use the Same Primitive

On a finite real interval, the same idea applies to definite integrals. For a complex-valued integrand $f$, if $F'=f$, then

$$
\int_u^v\operatorname{Im}f(x)\,dx
=\operatorname{Im}\bigl(F(v)-F(u)\bigr).
$$

For example, the first calculation gives

:::: {.equation-layout .equation-medium}
::: {.equation-wide}

$$
\int_0^\pi e^{2x}\sin x\,dx=\left[\frac{e^{2x}}5(2\sin x-\cos x)\right]_0^\pi=\frac{e^{2\pi}+1}{5}.
$$

:::
::: {.equation-narrow}

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\int_0^\pi e^{2x}\sin x\,dx\\
&\quad=\left[\frac{e^{2x}}5(2\sin x-\cos x)\right]_0^\pi\\
&\quad=\frac{e^{2\pi}+1}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

There is no integration constant to determine. We use the same primitive at both endpoints.

## What the Complex Form Reveals

The method keeps two structures visible. Sine and cosine are the two parts of one exponential. Polynomial derivatives form a finite list that eventually ends at zero.

Together, these facts turn the integration problem into a finite calculation. Complex multiplication keeps track of the changing sine and cosine coefficients. Repeated differentiation handles the polynomial factor. Products of trigonometric functions only introduce more frequencies to treat in the same way.
